chief_complaint: fever, flank pain, and vomiting in diabetic patient
hpi_details: A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with recently worsening fever, flank pain, vomiting, and generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he caught a severe stomach bug or ate bad food that disrupted his blood sugar control.
concerns: He is worried that his kidneys are failing from his diabetes and that he will be admitted to the hospital, leaving his dependent wife alone at home.
expectations: He hopes to get intravenous fluids and anti-nausea medicine today so he can keep his diabetes pills down and return home.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Complicated Pyelonephritis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

This presentation requires emergency assessment for sepsis and infected obstruction, including cultures, renal function, resuscitation, prompt empiric intravenous antibiotics tailored to local guidance and renal function, and urgent decompression if obstruction is present.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: fever, flank pain, and vomiting in diabetic patient
Key HPI features: a 65-year-old man with diabetes has worsening fever, flank pain, vomiting, and generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Complicated Pyelonephritis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Complicated Pyelonephritis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute pyelonephritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as sepsis, obstruction, or renal abscess.
management_principles: Admit for sepsis assessment, obtain urine and blood cultures, CBC and creatinine/eGFR, give fluids and renal-function-adjusted empiric IV antibiotics, and image urgently for obstruction or abscess; obtain urgent urologic decompression for infected obstruction.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of fever, flank pain, and vomiting in diabetic patient. HPI: complicated pyelonephritis.
reference_soap.objective: Assess vital signs, mental status, perfusion, urine output, CBC, creatinine/eGFR, lactate when septic, urinalysis/culture, and blood cultures before antibiotics when this does not delay treatment; obtain urgent imaging for obstruction or abscess.
reference_soap.assessment: Complicated pyelonephritis with high risk of sepsis and infected urinary obstruction in a patient with diabetes.
reference_soap.plan: Admit, resuscitate as indicated, and start renal-function-adjusted empiric IV antibiotics after cultures when feasible. Obtain urgent urology input for any obstructed infected system for drainage; do not delay decompression for antibiotic response.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Complicated Pyelonephritis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Complicated Pyelonephritis
Recognize complicated pyelonephritis as a sepsis/obstruction emergency requiring cultures, renal-function-aware antibiotics, imaging, and drainage when obstructed

teaching.one_liner: Upper urinary tract infection with increased risk of severe illness or treatment failure, such as in a patient with diabetes.
red_flags: Suspected urinary obstruction or renal abscess

must_ask.say: Have you had fever, shaking chills, confusion, or felt severely unwell?
Do you have burning when you urinate, urgency, frequency, or blood in your urine?
Where is the pain, and have nausea or vomiting prevented you from keeping fluids down?
Do you have diabetes, kidney disease, a urinary catheter, or any recent urinary procedure?
Are you passing much less urine, unable to urinate, or still feverish despite antibiotics?

history.answer: Doctor, I have a high fever, severe right flank pain, and I keep vomiting.
The fever and dull back pain started three days ago, but over the last 24 hours the pain became much worse and the vomiting began.
My thermometer at home read nearly 39 degrees yesterday evening, and I have had intense shaking chills.
I took some acetaminophen yesterday, but the fever barely budged and I threw up right after.
It is a constant, severe throbbing ache in my right lower back and side that doesn't let up.
I have vomited four times today and cannot keep down any food or liquids.
Yes, it burns when I urinate, and I have had to run to the bathroom frequently for small amounts of cloudy urine.
My urine has been cloudy and dark, but I haven't noticed visible red blood or passed any small stones.
No, I have never had kidney stones or episodes of urinary blockage before.
No, I have not had any urinary catheters or bladder procedures done.
No cough, phlegm, sore throat, or shortness of breath at all.
Aside from the vomiting and nausea, I do not have belly cramps or diarrhea.
No severe headache, neck stiffness, or confusion, though I feel completely exhausted and weak.
No, I have not noticed any rashes, insect bites, or black scabs on my body.
No drenching night sweats or unexplained weight loss before this started.
No, I haven't felt any swollen glands or lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
No recent travel outside the area, no hiking, no farm work, and no contact with animals.
No one around me has been sick; my wife is feeling completely fine.
No, I have never had chemotherapy or taken steroid medications or immune suppressants.
No artificial heart valves or heart disease, and I haven't had any dental work done recently.
No, I haven't started any new prescription medications or over-the-counter remedies.
I am in a monogamous relationship with my wife, with no new sexual partners, and I have never used intravenous drugs.
No pain in my groin or rectal area, and my urinary stream was normal before this started.
I was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes about seven years ago.
I had an appendectomy in my twenties, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I am currently not taking any medications; I had been trying to control my diabetes with diet alone.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked in my life.
I only have an occasional beer once or twice a month, but I haven't had any alcohol recently.
I am a retired accountant and I live at home with my wife.
My father had diabetes and high blood pressure, but no one in my family has had kidney disease.

I thought I just caught a bad stomach bug or food poisoning that was throwing my blood sugars completely out of control. With my diabetes, I'm scared my kidneys are shutting down and that being hospitalized will leave my wife all alone at home.
I'm hoping you can give me an IV for fluids and nausea so I can keep my diabetes pills down and sleep in my own bed tonight.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 104/66 mmHg, pulse 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, temperature 38.8°C, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Patient appears acutely ill, flushed, and diaphoretic, resting uncomfortably on the examination table.
Pharynx is clear without erythema or tonsillar exudate; oral mucous membranes appear somewhat dry.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy is palpable.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal chest excursion and no crackles or wheezes.
Tachycardic regular rate and rhythm with normal heart sounds; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is soft with mild deep tenderness in the right flank and right upper abdomen, without guarding or rigidity.
Marked percussion tenderness over the right costovertebral angle; left costovertebral angle is non-tender.
Warm and flushed without petechiae, purpura, rash, or eschar.
Neck is supple with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Normal anal sphincter tone; prostate is smooth, non-tender, and mildly enlarged without fluctuance.
